attributes.description: The capacity of a person to make informed, uncoerced, and independent choices about their own life, thoughts, and actions. In the context of AI, the way that the inputs, outputs, transmission and design of AI systems supports or undermines human autonomy. Also, the self-governance humans have over our own actions: Our authority to author our own intentions and actions.

The protection of human cognitive processes from hazardous influence; protecting the conditions under which people and groups reason for themselves as generative and agentic AI reshape attention, belief, memory, judgment, and agency. (Definition adopted from the [Cognitive Security Task Force](doc:ea042c2d-484d-4db8-a08b-ff373068b34e).)

In the context of AI, the capacity for people to think and act with AI in ways that increase their control, or the ability to shape the information environment; efficacy, or the capacity to act and think effectively with AI to pursue goals; and mastery, or the capacity to experience, learn, and grow durable capabilities through human-AI interaction over time. This definition includes both individual agency and collective agency, e.g., collective control has to do with access, portability and interoperability of information. (Definition adopted from [Taylor and Krishna, 2026](doc:7ae206d8-b677-4570-a419-8dcd48c78ecc).)

The enacted behavior of exercising intellectual independence in AI-rich environments. It manifests as the ability to set goals, validate outputs, and appropriately overrule the tool when necessary. Cognitive Sovereignty excludes mere influence; being persuaded by a well-reasoned argument (from a human or AI) is not a loss of sovereignty. (Definition adopted from [Klein and Klein, 2025](doc:6abe562e-48cd-44b8-a02f-48f04f710a8e).)

Another definition comes from [Konigsberg, 2026](doc:4c5b8a1a-132d-460c-838f-8d92de7baa07):  The capacity to (a) notice when one's thinking is being displaced (b) maintain a meaningful connection to how one's beliefs and judgments are formed, and (c) distinguish between genuine reasoning and the subjective impression of having reasoned.

The "right to mental self-determination", or cognitive liberty, is the freedom of an individual to control their own mental processes, cognition, and consciousness. Originally used in the context of neuroscience and related technologies that can monitor or influence consciousness, as well as the right of humans to influence their own consciousnesses (e.g., through yoga.) Now, in the context of AI, referenced when discussing AI systems that influence human perception, attention, decision-making, emotions, behavior and preferences, especially at scale.

nodes.label: The extended hollowed mind: why foundational knowledge is indispensable in the age of AI

attributes.title: The extended hollowed mind: why foundational knowledge is indispensable in the age of AI
attributes.summary:
In their 2025 paper on the "extended hollowed mind," Klein and Klein lay out a set of arguments for why it might not be so simple to keep thinking for yourself in the age of AI. They call it the "Sovereignty Trap", a reference to their term "cognitive sovereignty," or the ability to exercise intellectual independence in AI-rich environments. The points that make up the Trap are: 

1) Easy answers from LLMs undermine the processes our brains use to form strong knowledge bases, like retrieving information often and connecting new information to old.

2) Moreover, we prefer this, because cognitive effort is unpleasant and everything about chat-based LLM interactions is designed to be frictionless.  

3) Reduced effort around information actually changes how well we encode it. This means we either think we know something better than we do ("illusory knowledge"), or we're aware of our reduced command of information and no longer feel motivated to keep learning. 

Klein and Klein call the result of this Trap the hollowed mind: "A state of dependency where the frictionless availability of AI-generated answers enables users to systematically bypass the effortful cognitive processes essential for deep learning." In the Trap, not only do you fail to form robust knowledge schema, you're also disincentivized to interrogate an LLM's answers. This lack of effort further undermines your memory systems, and the next time you need to think for yourself, you are less competent and confident in doing so.
attributes.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) presents a fundamental duality for education: it simultaneously offers powerful cognitive extension while posing a significant risk of cognitive atrophy. This paper introduces the ‘hollowed mind’ as a conceptual framework to understand this risk—a state of dependency where the frictionless availability of AI-generated answers enables users to systematically bypass the effortful cognitive processes essential for deep learning. We argue this dynamic is driven by the ‘Sovereignty Trap’: a psychological mechanism where the AI’s authoritative competence tempts users to cede their own intellectual judgment, mistaking access to information for genuine ability. To substantiate this claim, we synthesize a multi-disciplinary body of evidence from cognitive science (e.g., dual-process theory, cognitive load), neurobiology (e.g., conflict-monitoring networks), and developmental psychology. We use this foundation to explain the widely documented ‘Expertise Duality’—why AI acts as a ‘leveler’ for novices but an ‘amplifier’ for experts. Moving beyond critique, this paper posits that the central challenge is one of environmental design, not user competence. We propose the ‘Fortified Mind’ as the pedagogical goal: a resilient internal architecture of indispensable knowledge and metacognitive skills required to achieve genuine ‘Cognitive Sovereignty’. Finally, we outline a forward-looking research agenda focused on redesigning AI tools from ‘answer engines’ into cognitive training environments that promote effortful engagement. Our work provides a robust conceptual guide for educators, researchers, and system designers, arguing that in the age of AI, the cultivation of fundamental knowledge is not just relevant, but more crucial than ever.

nodes.label: The Battle for Cognitive Liberty in the Age of Corporate AI

attributes.title: The Battle for Cognitive Liberty in the Age of Corporate AI
attributes.summary: Courtney Radsch argues that "a handful of corporations are redesigning the architecture of human thought into a system of cognitive capture" designed to influence what we see, think and feel. The increasing prevalence of AI and data collection about almost everything will lead to a mirror-world in which everything anticipates what you might want and works to persuade you of what you should think and do, from what products to buy to which politicians to support. Far from being unrealistic, Radsch's vision is just the AI version of what already happens today: Tech companies monopolize communication and media platforms to manipulate users' information access, beliefs and purchases. And opting out of these systems can be inconvenient or impossible, especially as the proliferation of AI leads to cognitive atrophy, reduced income for human creators and an increasingly polluted information landscape. Radsch argues that these outcomes are by design and that power concentration, surveillance and data capture are the goal, regardless of how helpful AI systems seem right now. Her conclusion is that protections for freedom of thought must be put into place immediately: "Without laws to protect freedom of thought, prohibit cognitive manipulation and require AI agents to act in the best interest of users; a market designed to make it unprofitable if not impossible to do otherwise; and competition to develop alternative rights-based AI products that are economically lucrative and socially beneficial, there is little to prevent this dystopian future."

nodes.label: Rethinking Cognitive Security in the Age of Generative AI

attributes.title: Rethinking Cognitive Security in the Age of Generative AI
attributes.summary:
The Cognitive Security Task Force says that "Cognitive security protects against unauthorized access to and hazardous influence over cognitive processes, such as perception, reasoning, decision-making, learning, and judgment. At its core, cognitive security refers to our ability to maintain sovereignty over our inner mental landscape, including our thoughts, feelings, subjective experiences, and dispositions. A cognitively secure world, then, supports human agency in deliberation, reflection, and sensemaking." They argue that though this idea isn't new (think about propaganda and advertising), it needs to be updated for the modern AI world, pointing at AI psychosis and personalized attacks on individuals as examples.

CSTF justifies the word "security" (over, e.g., liberty, another word in our ontology) because many of the things they are worried about are driven by malicious intent, e.g., mass disinformation. They also like that "security, in its technical lineage, implies ongoing attention to design, vulnerability, and repair." Their goal is to build robust standards and norms before we reach a "mass-adoption tipping point" where our minds are no longer considered sanctums.

nodes.label: Context-maxxing: A path to cognitive agency with generative AI

attributes.title: Context-maxxing: A path to cognitive agency with generative AI
attributes.summary:
This paper grounds "cognitive agency" in the broader tradition of human and sustainable development, drawing from Amartya Sen's work on human development as the "expansion of people's freedom to live lives they have reason to value" as well as Naila Kabeer's work on human empowerment and Elinor Ostrom's work on collective action. Whereas Sen, Kabeer and Ostrom were working in the context of the physical world, Taylor and Krishna define cognitive agency in the context of the digital world: The ability of people, individual and collective, to think and act within a digital environment shared with AI systems. They also define three pre-conditions: Control, or the ability to shape the information environment; efficacy, or the capacity to act and think effectively with AI to pursue goals; and mastery, or the capacity to experience, learn, and grow durable capabilities through human-AI interaction over time. One interesting thing about Taylor and Krishna's definitions is they include the collective, e.g., collective control has to do with access, portability and interoperability; collective efficacy requires a shared understanding of goals and cognitive diversity, etc.

The paper hinges on the OpenClaw movement, which allowed users to maintain much deeper control over their interaction environments than was ever possible before generative AI. The authors argue that this was an enormous shift: That, although the classic interfaces with generative AI are associated with loss of cognitive agency, and although the frontier labs are in a race to capture human context, generative AI has also provided an unprecedented opportunity for people to shape their own interfaces and keep control over their own context; and that the role of policy ought to be to codify, test and disseminate the emerging practices of this community. They focus on an approach they call "context-maxxing," or "using self-managed hardware and software to maximally control user-generated context to support interactions with generative AI."

The paper thus proposes a playbook for context-maxxing, with the claim that context-maxxing can help preserve and grow cognitive agency. It includes five infrastructure building blocks of context-maxxing (conditions for the "control" required for cognitive agency): A harness, or software that allows users to connect AI models to files, instructions, memory and tools; LLM access via API; a context web, or the information available across the user's digital surfaces; security measures; and hosting on hardware. They also provide suggestions for specification, orchestration and exploration, including the use of templates and ontologies (bolstering cognitive mastery), agent architectures and process decomposition (supporting cognitive efficacy), and reinvesting time once spent on grunt work in human-to-human interaction. To evaluate the effects of context-maxxing, the authors call for matched-task comparisons across architectures, longitudinal tracking, and collective-level analysis.

The paper closes by saying that increasing cognitive agency through context-maxxing could help people increase their ability to verify AI output (an advantage in today's economy) and protect worker agency by preventing context extraction. But the startup and infrastructure costs of context-maxxing today are quite high, suggesting policy moves are needed.
attributes.abstract: This working paper argues that generative AI should be assessed by whether it supports cognitive agency—or the capacity for people to think and act with AI in ways that increase their control, efficacy, and mastery. This account combines the foundational work in development economics (that identifies agency as central to human and sustainable development outcomes) with the latest research on socio-cognitive and informational agency to capture an emerging cognitive partnership between people and AI systems.

attributes.description: Cognitive atrophy, or a gradual loss or decline in cognitive ability that is not due to disease but rather to disuse or lack of mental challenge; in this context, specifically due to offloading cognitive effort onto AI. It is the “use‑it‑or‑lose‑it” counterpart to neuroplasticity; extended periods of low cognitive demand can shrink neural efficiency and lead to poorer performance on tasks that require working memory, fluid intelligence, etc.

"Thinking for ourselves" encompasses the terminology people are using to refer to the general ability of humans to perceive, think and decide for ourselves in the context of Large Language Models and other frontier AI. The definitions within this concept use different words (from cognitive liberty to cognitive security) and range from the individual to the collective, but are all concerned with how generative AI influences human cognition and our ability to navigate the world according to what's in our own heads.

nodes.label: Effects of AI use on human cognition

attributes.description: The effects of AI use on human cognition, including Large Language Models and other generative or frontier AI. This is specifically focused on individual effects, both short-term and longitudinal, such as the effects on memory of using LLMs, or how AI use changes problem-solving and higher-level judgment. How AI affects human cognition at all of the levels of Bloom's taxonomy (i.e., remembering up through analysis and creation) as well as longer-term aspects like persistence are all in scope.

Metacognitive laziness is learners’ tendency to offload effortful metacognitive self-regulatory practices, such as goal-setting, error monitoring, and strategic reflection, to AI systems rather than engaging in deliberate cognitive effort.

Cognitive offloading is the process by which humans delegate a cognitive task (e.g., remembering a phone number, solving a math problem) to an external system (a notebook, a PDA, a calculator, a partner). The external system acts as a “cognitive prosthetic,” freeing internal resources for higher‑order thinking.

attributes.title: Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice
attributes.summary: February 2026 numbers on how humans govern Claude behavior for simple and complex tasks. Interesting tidbit: "As agents and the science of agent measurement mature, the focus should be on whether humans are *in a position to effectively monitor and intervene*, rather than on requiring particular forms of involvement." (emphasis mine) The position seems to be that humans develop trust in Claude and shift from step-by-step approvals to general oversight, but the paper doesn't address how that shift affects human cognition other than saying it's important that interaction design not cause unnecessary friction.
attributes.abstract:
Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice
AI agents are here, and already they’re being deployed across contexts that vary widely in consequence, from email triage to cyber espionage. Understanding this spectrum is critical for deploying AI safely, yet we know surprisingly little about how people actually use agents in the real world.
We analyzed millions of human-agent interactions across both Claude Code and our public API using our privacy-preserving tool, to ask: How much autonomy do people grant agents? How does that change as people gain experience? Which domains are agents operating in? And are the actions taken by agents risky?
We found that:
- Claude Code is working autonomously for longer. Among the longest-running sessions, the length of time Claude Code works before stopping has nearly doubled in three months, from under 25 minutes to over 45 minutes. This increase is smooth across model releases, which suggests it isn’t purely a result of increased capabilities, and that existing models are capable of more autonomy than they exercise in practice.
- Experienced users in Claude Code auto-approve more frequently, but interrupt more often. As users gain experience with Claude Code, they tend to stop reviewing each action and instead let Claude run autonomously, intervening only when needed. Among new users, roughly 20% of sessions use full auto-approve, which increases to over 40% as users gain experience.
- Claude Code pauses for clarification more often than humans i

attributes.title: Brave New Nudge
attributes.summary: McCord argues that AI systems can increase agency – our ability to act to get what we want – while degrading autonomy, our ability to determine what we want. A system that makes better choices than we ever could will erode our capacity for choice and our very dignity while still possibly improving our well-being over time. Moreover, AI systems are not guaranteed to make these better choices because much of what it means to be human is to self-author – and the more we defer to the choice a machine makes, the less our own preferences are actually driving the choice.

attributes.title: Well-Being, Agency and Freedom: The Dewey Lectures 1984
attributes.summary: These are lectures given by Amartya Sen, an economist and philosopher who has worked in many contexts including welfare economics, social choice theory and famine. I include these lectures as context for Taylor and Krishna's definition of cognitive agency. In them, Sen defines "agency freedom" and identifies two components, one of which seems related to other philosophers' views of human autonomy.
attributes.abstract: The main aim of Dewey lectures is to explore a moral approach that sees persons from two different perspectives: and agency. Both the well-being aspect and the agency aspect of persons have their own relevance in the assessment of states and actions. A second objective is to examine a set of metaethical issues, making use of an approach to moral analysis which focuses on the admissibility and use of different types of information in moral valuation. Informational analysis can be used to bring out the content, scope, and limitations of different moral principles. A few examples may help to illustrate the diversity of ways in which informational constraints may be used through the specification of invariance requirements. Authorship invariance does have some claims to being a reasonable requirement of moral evaluation. The possibility of combining position relativity with authorship invariance is also the reason why positionality of moral valuation is perfectly consistent with objectivity of moral values.

nodes.label: A Framework for Measuring Human Cognitive Agency Amid Routine AI Adoption

attributes.title: A Framework for Measuring Human Cognitive Agency Amid Routine AI Adoption
attributes.abstract: The rapid integration of large language models into everyday cognitive tasks writing, reasoning, decision-making, and professional judgmenthas created an urgent need for frameworks that capture the cognitive consequences of delegating thinking to AI systems. Existing constructs in psychology and education, including critical thinking, metacognition, intellectual autonomy, and epistemic agency, each address related phenomena but none adequately describes the specic capacity threatened by habitual AI-assisted cognition: the ability to remain the genuine author of one's own understanding. This paper introduces cognitive sovereignty as a distinct psychological construct, defined as the capacity to (a) notice when one's thinking is being displaced (b) maintain a meaningful connection to how one's beliefs and judgments are formed, and (c) distinguish between genuine reasoning and the subjective impression of having reasoned. I trace the concept's philosophical lineage, dierentiate it from adjacent constructs through systematic comparison, propose a ve-dimensional model (Authorship Awareness, Process Ownership, Source Discrimination, Capacity Maintenance, and Delegation Discernment), present a nomological network with predicted relations to existing measures, and outline a measurement instrument: the Cognitive Sovereignty Scale (CSS), with candidate items and a multi-phase validation strategy. We conclude with specic, testable predictions that follow from the framework. We argue that cognitive sovereignty names a phenomenon that existing constructs individually fail to capture and that its operationalization is a prerequisite for empirical research on the cognitive consequences of AI adoption.

nodes.label: “You shall have the thought”: habeas cogitationem as a New Legal Remedy to Enforce Freedom of Thinking and Neurorights

attributes.title: “You shall have the thought”: habeas cogitationem as a New Legal Remedy to Enforce Freedom of Thinking and Neurorights
attributes.summary: In the tradition of *habeas corpus*, the authors propose *habeas cogitationem* as "a prerogative writ used to challenge the validity of a neurotechnological interference in a person's thought process, either in official or private hands." They give many examples of neurorights that would be enforced by such a writ, e.g., the right of a person not to be algorithmically discriminated against by an insurance algorithm using facial data collected to diagnose Parkinson's. While the paper is largely out of scope for this Field Guide at the moment, I recommend it as a review of neurorights in the context of neurotechnologies.
attributes.abstract: Abstract Despite its obvious advantages, the disruptive development of neurotechnology can pose risks to fundamental freedoms. In the context of such concerns, proposals have emerged in recent years either to design human rights de novo or to update the existing ones. These new rights in the age of neurotechnology are now widely referred to as “neurorights.” In parallel, there is a considerable amount of ongoing academic work related to updating the right to freedom of thought in order to include the protection of “freedom of thinking” (i.e., freedom of thought itself) and not only its social manifestations. Neurorights such as cognitive liberty, free will, mental freedom, and mental self-determination come into play here. Importantly, freedom of thought has often been considered a prerequisite for all the other fundamental freedoms and rights. In any case, just as other rights require additional legal instruments to guarantee their compliance, substantial neurorights will probably require specific complementary developments in procedural law. In relation to this, there is a long tradition of habeas corpus as an emergency remedy to enforce the rights of a citizen against illegal or arbitrary detention. More recently, the habeas data writ has been proposed and admitted in certain countries to guarantee a person’s ownership of their personal data. In this article, we propose to expand this procedural apparatus by incorporating a third habeas, which we call habeas cogitationem : a writ aimed primarily at enforcing the right to freedom of thinking (and, subsidiarily, the rest of neurorights) against direct, harmful interferences in a person’s thought process by both public and private perpetrators.

nodes.label: A Conceptual Framework to Safeguard the Neuroright to Personal Autonomy

attributes.title: A Conceptual Framework to Safeguard the Neuroright to Personal Autonomy
attributes.summary: This paper is another framework for parsing exactly what rights we *have* when it comes to thinking for ourselves. The authors bring up a range of concerns around "free will" as the neuroright designated to protect personal autonomy. They also compare free will (the "right to have ultimate control over [one's] own decision-making, without unknown manipulation from external neurotechnologies") to cognitive liberty (the "right to alter one's mental states with the help of neurotools as well as to refuse to do so") and suggest that some of the confusion around these terms is because our understanding of human action is impoverished. I particularly appreciate their bringing in Pacherie's action theory, which differentiates intentions, deliberations, decisions, and the "realization of actions." They conclude by proposing a definition of personal autonomy that aligns closely with [McCord's](doc:163500a9-23d2-443e-94e6-990f76410362) and comes with two conditions: That the person requests or authorizes intervention, and that they are fully informed about the behavioral consequences of that intervention.
attributes.abstract: Abstract In this article, we propose a philosophical exploration on the main problems involved in two neurorights that concern autonomous action, namely free will and cognitive liberty, and sketch a possible solution to these problems by resourcing to a holistic interpretation of human actions. First, we expose the main conceptual and practical issues arising from the neuroright to “free will,” which are far from minor: the term itself is denied by some trends participating in the neurorights debate, the related concept of ultimate control is also disputed, the understanding of free will depends on cultural context, and the exercise of being free to act in several domains may be covered by other regulations. Second, we analyze the historical origin of cognitive liberty, its current status, and its relation with free will. Third, we criticize the concept of decision in mainstream action theory and propose to conceive action as a unified process constituted by three explanatory, non-sequential dimensions: intention, decision, and action realization. Fourth, we discuss two possible cases involving neurotechnologies and suggest ways to interpret them according to a unified framework in which free will and cognitive liberty fall under a single neuroright to personal autonomy. Finally, we outline a recommendation to introduce freedom of thought and personal autonomy as complementary neurorights to protect both the internal and external dimensions of thought and action.

nodes.label: The fundamental rights risks of countering cognitive warfare with artificial intelligence

attributes.title: The fundamental rights risks of countering cognitive warfare with artificial intelligence
attributes.summary:
This paper frames government efforts to fight disinformation as potentially paternalistic and counter to "citizens' fundamental rights in liberal-democratic political systems." "Cognitive warfare", i.e., non-kinetic warfare relying on information and communication technologies, has been around for a while; recent election interference, for example, counts as cognitive warfare, and the authors bring up COVID-19 misinformation as well. Of course, the advent of generative AI threatens to make the problem much worse as human-like content, including deepfakes, can now be generated at massive scales. The authors are mainly concerned with new efforts by EU and NATO policymakers to protect citizens from cognitive warfare, including misinformation campaign detection projects and automated moderation tactics where machines correct misinformation across platforms. They claim that while this type of activity is fine for corporations to do as they have contracts with their users, for the state to do so amounts to "epistemic paternalism" and must be evaluated more carefully. Their main concerns are:

1. Training AI systems to detect cognitive warfare may interfere with privacy and data protection rights.
2. Using these systems may impact communication rights, i.e., freedoms of expression, information and the media.
3. The risk of being silenced by these systems may reduce the diversity of media and information sources in a society and limit collective decision-making opportunities (i.e., "any government intervention with the help of AI to decide what information is acceptable infringes on the process of political will-formation itself and thus implicates the right to self-determination.")

The authors close by claiming that the link between sustained disinformation campaigns and actual behavior change, e.g., in elections, hasn't been solidly established in the literature yet, and thus justifying state-controlled AI mediation can really only be done via the precautionary principle (i.e., "if this is bad it's going to be **real** bad, so we ought to do something about it before we have all the information.")
attributes.abstract: This article analyses ideas to use AI-supported systems to counter 'cognitive warfare' and critically examines the implications of such systems for fundamental rights and values. After explicating the notion of 'cognitive warfare' as used in contemporary public security discourse, the article describes the emergence of generative AI tools that are expected to exacerbate the problem of adversarial activities against the online information ecosystems of democratic societies. In response, researchers and policymakers have proposed to utilize AI to devise countermeasures, ranging from AI-based early warning systems to state-run content moderation tools. These interventions, however, interfere, to different degrees, with fundamental rights and values such as privacy, communication rights, and self-determination. This article argues that such proposals insufficiently account for the complexity of contemporary online information ecosystems, particularly the inherent difficulty in establishing causality and attribution. Reliance on the precautionary principle might offer a justificatory frame for AI-enabled measures to counter 'cognitive warfare' in the absence of conclusive empirical evidence of harm. However, any such state intervention must be based in law and adhere to strict proportionality.

nodes.label: Mental integrity, autonomy, and fundamental interests

attributes.title: Mental integrity, autonomy, and fundamental interests
attributes.summary:
This paper sits again in the context of neurotechnology or neuromodulation: "targeted energetic intervention in the brain using electrical, magnetic or other forms of stimulation." While this Guide focuses more on LLMs, UIs and other non-zapping technologies, it's useful to read work by neuroethicists because the terminology overlap is large. In this paper, Zuk is concerned with *mental integrity*. 

Zuk reviews definitions of mental integrity, most of which begin with autonomy (the "autonomy-based conception.") Some theorists define mental integrity as being about control or authority over one's own mind, either over the contents or the sources of influence on those contents. Others say that mental integrity is a state, i.e., the absence of influences on or interference with our autonomous preferences. (This control-versus-state difference is similarly found in the agency literature – recall that in [The Cognitives](node:32594bc2-e59a-4c3b-b02a-dbee7629e827), "agency freedom" and "agency" are somewhat interchangeable.) Regardless of whether mental integrity is a state or a form of control, Zuk points out that these definitions are weaker than they could be because "interference is ubiquitous." What's to differentiate, for example, the interference of you talking to me in a conversation from you pointing a transcranial magnetic stimulation device at me? 

Rather than discuss mental integrity in terms of specific interference and specific preferences, Zuk proposes that it could be a precondition of autonomy, a "general capacity to form and enact autonomous preferences and to consent." He argues that this definition leads to a more defendable right to mental integrity – that is, the right to mental integrity is violated when the following capacities are undermined:

1. Our capacity for affect, i.e., our ability to "experience certain feelings." So, for example, being tranquilized against our will might be a violation of mental integrity via the diminishment of our affective interests.
2. Our capacity for cognition and "the epistemic interests it grounds." Zuk takes the position that "we have a second set of interests in our capacity as *inquirers* attempting to make sense of the world and our place in it, often in concert with others." So, for example, the pollution of the information environment by LLM paper mills might be a violation of our mental integrity, or an [LLM designed to subtly gaslight us](node:60da85f4-8630-4076-b0cc-bc5697f785c5), or even an algorithm designed to disrupt our attention spans and make rational reflection more difficult.
3. Our capacity for agency, i.e., to intend or will and act accordingly. We talk quite a bit about agency in [The Cognitives](node:32594bc2-e59a-4c3b-b02a-dbee7629e827) and Zuk does not throw any curveballs here.

So Zuk's definition of mental integrity is that it is violated "when the *capacities underlying* fundamental interests are bypassed, eroded, overwhelmed, or otherwise undermined." Taking our example from earlier, when you and I are having a conversation, your tone may cheer me up or bum me out (changing my affect), and the content of the conversation may influence what I believe (an epistemic influence), but the conversation does not violate my mental integrity because my *capacities* to feel and believe are not affected. By contrast, if you're pointing a TMS device at me designed to activate parts of my brain that make me feel excited, you are undermining my capacity to govern my own affect, which *could* be a violation of mental integrity (especially if, e.g., you're also trying to sell me a timeshare.) Or, more realistically, it is also a violation of mental integrity if we have many conversations over time in which you gaslight me and undermine my capacity to form beliefs. Zuk's examples are particularly relevant to the concerns of this Field Guide: He classifies an onslaught of upsetting posts, pervasive misinformation, and algorithms that erode our attention spans as violations of mental integrity.

Zuk's last point concerns the conditions under which violating mental integrity is wrong. He gives an example of a woman who sees a factory farming video and is upset for the rest of the day. Zuk's position is that it is wrong to "violate mental integrity *for no good reason*," but kicks the "good reason" can down the road.
attributes.abstract: Many technology ethicists hold that the time has come to articulate neurorights : our normative claims vis-à-vis our brains and minds. One such claim is the right to mental integrity (‘MI’). I begin by considering some paradigmatic threats to MI (§1) and how the dominant autonomy-based conception (‘ABC’) of MI attempts to make sense of them (§2). I next consider the objection that the ABC is overbroad in its understanding of what threatens MI and suggest a friendly revision to the ABC that addresses the objection (§3). I then consider a second objection: that the ABC cannot make sense of the MI of the non-autonomous . This objection appears fatal even to the revised ABC (§4). On that basis, I develop an alternative conception on which MI is grounded in a plurality of simpler capacities, namely, those for affect , cognition , and volition . Each of these more basic capacities grounds a set of fundamental interests, and they are for that reason worthy of protection even when they do not rise to the level of complexity necessary for autonomy (§5). This yields a fully general theory of MI that accounts for its manifestations in both the autonomous and the non-autonomous.

attributes.title: Cognitive sovereignty and neurocomputational harm in predictive digital platforms
attributes.summary: I could not tell the difference between LLM writing and the writing in this paper. But it does make an interesting point that the design of sports betting platforms can undermine cognitive sovereignty and are a tractable area to test out policy on that topic. In particular, Atkinson focuses on "tempo," making the argument that algorithms can mess with your brain's sense of timing such that not acting can feel bad. He also argues that, seeing as platforms can tell when a person is vulnerable, not applying safeguards is a form of negligence.

attributes.title: Achieving Cognitive Liberty (book review)
attributes.summary: This is a review of The Battle for Your Brain, a book by neuroethicist and law professor Nita Farahany. The book focuses on neurotechnology as a threat to cognitive liberty, which is slightly outside the scope of this Guide at the moment – but the review is short and sweet, worth a peek to see what the neurotechnologists are thinking about.
attributes.abstract: Neurotechnologies necessitate new thinking on human rights.

nodes.label: Dropping Anchor in Rough Seas: Co-Reasoning with Personalized AI Advisors and the Liberalism of Fear

attributes.title: Dropping Anchor in Rough Seas: Co-Reasoning with Personalized AI Advisors and the Liberalism of Fear
attributes.summary:
I liked this paper a lot, particularly as an elaboration on McCord's [piece about human autonomy](doc:163500a9-23d2-443e-94e6-990f76410362) and as an exploration of the cognitive aspects of gradual disempowerment. Queloz is responding to an earlier piece by Benjamin Lang describing how personalized AI advisors can strike the right balance between fidelity to a user's established normative values and flexibility to recalibrate as those values evolve. Queloz argues that, even if such a model could be perfectly designed, Lang is an optimist when it comes to political contexts; and the risks change when one applies Judith Shklar's "liberalism of fear." 

Shklar's liberalism of fear argues that, rather than asking how we might optimize towards utopia, our first question ought to be: "How do we prevent the worst things that humans predictably end up doing to one another when armed with power?" Put another way: "Before we maximize the odds of self-realization, we should minimize the odds of domination by others." This feels **so relevant** to ongoing discussions about AI today. The leaders of the big labs are relentless in their claims of self-realization – take Meta's recent manifesto, which directly asks whether AI will be a "tool that empowers everyone" and claims that "everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about." We could take that at face value, or, in Shklar's tradition, we could remind ourselves of Meta's past and ongoing campaigns to concentrate power and attention across its platforms, and ask how we should design these agents to prevent damage on an unprecedented scale. 

Queloz gives some great examples of why we should worry about personal agents even if Lang's design "works." One in particular is [the example that got me started in this area](doc:60da85f4-8630-4076-b0cc-bc5697f785c5): The asymmetric information that personal agents have about us compared to our squishy and fallible brains could make us feel that their authority is primary (i.e., your LLM can gaslight you.) Another is the fear that "what looks like co-reasoning at [time] *t* can be part of a long arc of 'soft steering,' though the pattern may be so subtle that it is discernible only over many years and across many users." That is, entire populations could be nudged towards, e.g., a preference for dictatorship, and we would only be able to detect and prosecute that pattern once it took effect at massive scales over a long period of time. I'll add a note here, too, that this steering needn't even be malicious or intentional, though that's what Queloz is worried about; for example, [Kulveit et al.'s paper on gradual disempowerment](doc:cdd59efc-5156-4be5-ae3c-d6880998e7c7) doesn't require malicious intention either from humans or AIs.

To close, Queloz lays out some minimum requirements to avoid personal AI advisors becoming "technologies of soft governance":

1. The design of these advisors should first protect users from domination before maximizing self-realization. That means that, say, we should avoid aggregating data that can be bought by law enforcement and can't be deleted, even if that means the advisors function less well.
2. Operational norms (how advisors "treat trade-offs between, say, conformity and dissent, self-sacrifice and self-care, prudence and solidarity") should be publicly contestable and controllable.
3. The recognition that some burdens, e.g., "the burden of resisting cruel institutions," are *civic* burdens. Queloz writes, "a liberalism of fear will therefore be sceptical of any technology whose primary contribution is to help individuals adjust to life in unjust conditions." 

Although Queloz and Lang's pieces both focus on normative decision-making and self-realization, I think the requirements above apply across domains. For example, the requirement around contestability of operational norms brings to mind Deep Mind's Habermas Machine, which makes choices about the priority of consensus over dissent that we didn't sign off on. And the last point calls to mind [Ferdman's argument](doc:af3bc2ac-d3f0-43e5-aa88-d657c818c8c8) that AI deskilling is a structural problem – an agent helping you decide, for example, what work is still available to you could be used to dampen widespread unrest about skill decay and job loss. In general I found this piece to be short, sweet and useful – would recommend you take a peek yourself.
attributes.abstract: Abstract In response to Benjamin Lang’s defence of “co-reasoning” with personalized AI advisors, this article formulates a political critique of the co-reasoning model through the lens of the liberalism of fear. This reframes the ethical aspiration to self-realization with the assistance of AI by embedding it within a realistic political setting. It suggests that before we seek to maximize the odds of self-realization, we should strive to minimize the odds of domination by others. After highlighting three power asymmetries involved in the co-reasoning model, the article argues that personalization risks stabilizing domination by translating structural injustices into individualized aspirational challenges. Three political constraints on personalized AI are then proposed: the priority of non-domination, the public contestability of operative norms, and the recognition of non-personalizable civic burdens.

nodes.label: Freedom of Thought and Digital Technologies: Operationalizing State Obligations for Social Media, Virtual Reality, and Neurotechnology

attributes.title: Freedom of Thought and Digital Technologies: Operationalizing State Obligations for Social Media, Virtual Reality, and Neurotechnology
attributes.summary:
The aim of this paper is to clarify and operationalize the right to "freedom of thought" in the context of digital technologies. Bublitz takes an approach I'm starting to recognize (see, e.g., [this paper](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4)), where he avoids messy problems like how to define and scope such a right in favor of clarifying its *preconditions.* He begins by explaining that freedom of thought appears in many human rights treaties and that states are obligated not only to *not* interfere with people's thoughts but to protect people *from* interference, e.g., at the hands of companies. However, because "thought" is hard to define and interference is not justifiable under these treaties, case law is remarkably lacking. And digital technologies aren't likely to clear the bar of severity (e.g., seeing a single personalized advertisement) – plus, we use them voluntarily.

Rather than focus on specific harms, Bublitz reframes the problem as the state's obligation to "fulfil conditions for the full enjoyment of the right [to freedom of thought]." He lays out ten aspects of freedom of thought based on discourse going back to Voltaire, which, at risk of a lengthy summary, I think are worth replicating here:

1. Thinking for oneself (the core definition)
2. Freedom from external influence (a prerequisite)
3. The ability to think independently and make up one's own mind
4. "Free" thinking, i.e., creative, innovative, flexible, etc.
5. Critical thinking, i.e., skepticism, belief revision, etc.
6. Rational thought or reasoning
7. The freedom to seek the truth (not the right not to be lied to, but the freedom to discern true from false)
8. Free decision-making, i.e., if I am liable for my decisions and presumed to have made them freely, the law must also safeguard that freedom
9. Control of attention
10. Privacy of thought, i.e., protection from digital and bio-surveillance

Bublitz then reviews three examples of technologies that may impact freedom of thought: Neurotechnologies (e.g., reconstructing inner dialogue using brain data and machine learning algorithms), virtual reality (i.e., an environment that potentially totally and "systematically frustrates the search for truth") and social media (i.e., at the opposite end of the spectrum from virtual reality in that it is not "one overwhelming immersive experience but a multitude of innocuous stimuli.") He narrows in on concerns about social media, namely that it weakens attention and reflective thinking, creates "subtle forms of addiction," and warps the ways we form beliefs (e.g., repeated exposure to statements increases perceived truthfulness.) Addressing these concerns legally, though, comes with some challenges:

1. Attention capture could be seen as rights interference...but attention disruption is ubiquitous and easily trivialized. (This is the same concern Zuk holds in his [paper on mental integrity](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4).) What's more, users use social media voluntarily – we all sign agreements that give our consent for advertising – which means that we can't usually say our rights have been infringed upon.
2. Social media harms are a "many hands" problem, i.e., it is very hard / implausible to link a specific harm to a specific actor.

Which brings Bublitz back to the obligation to *fulfill*, i.e., not only to enforce rights but to promote the preconditions for the enjoyment of rights. He argues that, though specific harms can't easily be attributed to specific actors, the *aggregate* harms from social media still exist; and, on top of that, avoiding social media in this day and age can cause harm in other parts of a person's life, e.g., social exclusion.<Footnote>Side note – how come I need a Twitter account to get, e.g., news from my local government officials?</Footnote> So *fulfilling* freedom of thought may require regulation of the digital environment, just as fulfilling the right to water requires controlling water quality. He makes a final argument that, while state limitations on technology use is paternalistic, "mandating companies to provide better products...is not," particularly as the detrimental effects of voluntary use are often regretted by users and that the market currently doesn't *offer* alternatives to products that have those side effects.
attributes.abstract: Abstract Freedom of thought is among the strongest human rights, yet it is largely devoid of practical legal application. This article operationalizes the right by distilling ten core aspects, mainly psychological capacities such as attention, meta-control over thought, and rational belief formation. It then examines how these aspects may be adversely affected by three digital technologies: neurotechnologies, virtual reality, and especially social media. The article addresses why the use of digital technologies might be a human rights issue at all and the doctrinal challenge associated with it. People use these technologies voluntarily, and detrimental effects tend to arise from a multitude of diffuse stimuli rather than from discrete identifiable interventions by a specific human -rights-bound actor. This complicates, and often renders impossible, findings of conventional interferences with rights. But this may not exhaust the remit of human rights. Another human rights-based perspective is proposed: Detrimental effects on thought might be conceptualized as risks arising from a digital environment, which may prompt States’ obligations to fulfil the enjoyment of the right by securing its factual–in this case, psychological–preconditions. A prime measure to meet this obligation is the regulation of technology through innovative models such as a freedom-of-thought impact assessment, or freedom-of-thought-sensitive technology design, for which the ten aspects provide a workable foundation.

nodes.label: The Cambridge Handbook of the Right to Freedom of Thought

attributes.title: The Cambridge Handbook of the Right to Freedom of Thought
attributes.summary: I have not read this book! It is too far out of the scope of this guide. But if you find yourself interested in the law and freedom of thought, this seems like the thing to read. It's got chapters on many different countries' treatment of freedom of thought.
attributes.abstract: The right to freedom of thought features prominently in debates about emerging technologies including neurotechnology and AI, but there is little understanding of its scope, content or application. This handbook presents the first attempt to set out how the right is protected, interpreted and applied globally. Eighteen jurisdictions are examined along with chapters describing context-setting, interdisciplinary approaches, and close analysis of the right in relation to specific challenges and conceptual difficulties. Readers familiar with the right will discover fresh perspectives and those new to the right will learn how it is part of the matrix of rights protecting autonomy, dignity, and privacy.

nodes.label: Towards a Human Right to Psychological Continuity? Reflections on the Rights to Personal Identity, Self-Determination, and Personal Integrity

attributes.title: Towards a Human Right to Psychological Continuity? Reflections on the Rights to Personal Identity, Self-Determination, and Personal Integrity
attributes.summary: This paper argues that there is no need for a distinct right to psychological continuity as it is already covered by existing protections.
attributes.abstract: Abstract Scholars from different disciplines are increasingly debating how human rights should protect the autonomy not only over our bodies but also over our minds. These debates are often driven by emerging technologies that appear able to access, monitor, and manipulate mental states in ways that were previously inconceivable. Whereas some human rights already protect certain personal interests in the mental realm, such as the right to freedom of thought, it has been argued that new or updated human rights are necessary to offer adequate protection against modern technologies that may threaten our mental privacy, personal integrity, and identity. One of the proposed rights, which is under consideration by the Council of Europe and the UN Human Rights Council, concerns a right to ‘psychological continuity’. This paper challenges the necessity of recognising such a right, arguing that the notion of psychological continuity already receives considerable protection within the established framework of human rights law.
attributes.publication: The European Convention on Human Rights Law Review

nodes.label: Persuasive Technology and computational manipulation: hypernudging out of mental self-determination

attributes.title: Persuasive Technology and computational manipulation: hypernudging out of mental self-determination
attributes.summary: This paper links historical discussions on privacy and cognitive liberty to new legislation in Europe and from the U.N. around persuasive AI technologies. Faraoni argues that these technologies can *manipulate* us, i.e., cause us to change our preferences, decisions or actions without engaging our rational or deliberative capacities, and while manipulation has always been part of our lives, the scale, speed and accuracy of AI-driven systems is unprecedented.<Footnote>Faraoni argues that AI technologies can create "extremely accurate cognitive profile[s]" of users, which...citation needed, I'm going to look into that. AI is not described precisely in this paper.</Footnote> Faraoni reviews existing legislation around computational manipulation and "informational self-determination", i.e., the authority we hold to decide what information about our private lives should be available to others. He then reviews the literature on mental integrity and cognitive liberty and argues that "hypernudging" via an AI system violates our right to mental self-determination. I would recommend the paper as a good review of the arguments in this area – I don't think it advances any of those arguments significantly but aims to bring them together in the context of AI systems.
attributes.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, unperceived, can acquire the user's data, find connections not visible by a human being, profile the users, and aim at persuading them, resulting in Persuasive Technology (PT). During the persuasive process, PT can use manipulation, finding and using routes to affect System 1, the primordial brain of individuals, in the absence of their awareness, undermining their decision-making processes. Multiple international and European bodies recognized that AI systems could use manipulation at an unprecedented degree via second-generation dark patterns such as the hypernudge and that computational manipulation constitutes a risk for autonomy and different, overlapping, fundamental rights such as privacy, informational self-determination and freedom of thought. However, there is a lack of shared ideas regarding which fundamental rights are violated by computational manipulation and which fundamental rights can protect individuals against it. The right to be let alone and the right to hold and express a thought differ from the right to create a thought, being in control of the decision-making process and free from cognitive interferences operated by computational manipulation. Therefore, this paper argues in favor of recognizing a newly emerged fundamental right, the right to mental self-determination, tailored to the unprecedented abilities of AI-driven manipulative technologies.

nodes.label: Minding Rights: Mapping Ethical and Legal Foundations of ‘Neurorights’

attributes.title: Minding Rights: Mapping Ethical and Legal Foundations of ‘Neurorights’
attributes.summary: This paper is a multi-disciplinary effort to "map the ethical and legal foundations of neurorights with the purpose to facilitate international discussions and policy initiatives at various levels." They are focused on neurotechnologies, i.e., devices that can monitor and/or intervene in brain activity. The authors acknowledge the ongoing debate about whether specific neurorights are needed, e.g., a specific right to mental privacy or cognitive liberty, and examine the extent to which these things are already protected under current law. Their review claims that the right to mental integrity exists under international and regional law, as does the right to freedom of thought; that the right to mental privacy has not yet been recognized but may be implicit in the rights to privacy, freedom of thought and freedom of expression; and that cognitive liberty is more often seen as a bundle of rights, some of which already exist.
attributes.abstract: The rise of neurotechnologies, especially in combination with artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods for brain data analytics, has given rise to concerns around the protection of mental privacy, mental integrity and cognitive liberty - often framed as "neurorights" in ethical, legal, and policy discussions. Several states are now looking at including neurorights into their constitutional legal frameworks, and international institutions and organizations, such as UNESCO and the Council of Europe, are taking an active interest in developing international policy and governance guidelines on this issue. However, in many discussions of neurorights the philosophical assumptions, ethical frames of reference and legal interpretation are either not made explicit or conflict with each other. The aim of this multidisciplinary work is to provide conceptual, ethical, and legal foundations that allow for facilitating a common minimalist conceptual understanding of mental privacy, mental integrity, and cognitive liberty to facilitate scholarly, legal, and policy discussions.

nodes.label: The Right to Mental Integrity: Multidimensional, Multilayered and Extended

attributes.title: The Right to Mental Integrity: Multidimensional, Multilayered and Extended
attributes.summary: This is a useful review of prevailing thought around mental integrity and mental privacy, focusing again on neurotechnologies, e.g., the case of a woman whose brain implant was forcibly removed.
attributes.abstract: Abstract In this article I present a characterization of the right to mental integrity (RMI), expanding and refining the definition proposed by Ienca and Andorno’s ( Life Science Society Policy 13 5, 2017) and clarifying how the scope of this right should be shaped in cases of cognitive extension (EXT). In doing so, I will first critically survey the different formulations of the RMI presented in the literature. I will then argue that the RMI protects from i) nonconsensual interferences that ii) bypass reasoning and iii) produce mental harm . Contrary to other definitions proposed in the literature, my formulation disentangles the RMI from the right to cognitive liberty (RCL) (Lavazza in Frontiers Neuroscience 12 82, 2018), the right to mental privacy (RMP) (Lavazza and Giorgi in Neuroethics 16 (1): 1-13, 2023), and the right to psychological continuity (RPC) (Zohny et al. in Neuroethics 16: 20, 2023), thus enabling a fine-grained assessment of their simultaneous or individual violation. Finally, I analyse how the extended mind thesis (EXT) reshapes the scope of the RMI, proposing a layered protection of extended mental integrity, which grants stronger protection to the organism-bound cognitive system and self in case of manipulative influences of the mind-extending device. To conclude, I present a variety of neurorights violations and mental harms inflicted to organism-bound and cognitively extended agents.

nodes.label: Making Tangible the Long-Term Harm Linked to the Chilling Effects of AI-enabled Surveillance: Can Human Flourishing Inform Human Rights?

attributes.title: Making Tangible the Long-Term Harm Linked to the Chilling Effects of AI-enabled Surveillance: Can Human Flourishing Inform Human Rights?
attributes.summary:
Like the [paper on co-reasoning with AI advisors](node:8af7601e-750a-4345-b320-dcc2458df1fe), this article concerns itself with self-realization and "human flourishing" in the context of AI-enabled surveillance. The authors don't really describe AI-enabled surveillance beyond pointing out that being watched by anything  can have a chilling effect on the decisions individuals make. But I think it's worth a scroll through the summary because a) AI-enabled surveillance is real, from social media tracking to the absolute evil garbage fire that are Flock cameras, and b) this paper brings in a couple of approaches we've seen in other contexts, including [cognitive agency](node:5e159bca-4bd9-4d59-9c20-f14330863563) and [discussions of deskilling](node:af3bc2ac-d3f0-43e5-aa88-d657c818c8c8).

They first examine the arguments of Aristotle, Philippa Foot and Rosalind Hursthouse, who say that human flourishing can be objectively determined (i.e., "top-down") and includes our ability to live rationally (i.e., "any way that we can rightly see as good, as something *we have reason to do.*") Acting rightly requires developing virtues such as justice, generosity and so on – but states can fail in their duty to help citizens develop these virtues.<Footnote>This should sound familiar to [Ferdman's argument](node:af3bc2ac-d3f0-43e5-aa88-d657c818c8c8) that capacity-hostile environments can contribute to deskilling beyond the control of any individual and that this undermines our flourishing.</Footnote> The authors then acknowledge that this view of top-down virtues reduces [autonomy](node:5bb1bd8f-935d-4458-917c-1ff780825a93) – Foot, for example, says that people can't choose the virtues against which to decide their actions – which is therefore at odds with the emphasis of human rights law on individual agency and dignity.

L.W. Sumner, on the other hand, proposes a subjective (i.e., "bottom-up") perspective on human flourishing that merely requires a person's "life-satisfaction assessment" to be informed and autonomous. Basically: Unless you can show someone has been brainwashed, you must take at face value their assessment of their own happiness. But, of course, brainwashing is only the most extreme form of "corrupting" someone's autonomy, and Sumner doesn't really deal with the subtler cases of influence (think, say, persistent misinformation on social media, or gaslighting from an LLM.)

So, if the objective approach threatens autonomy and the subjective approach requires difficult definitions, how should we think about the potential effects of AI surveillance? The authors finally propose the capabilities approach, first introduced by [Amartya Sen](node:c8a9c7e6-ce04-489b-9df2-171102fa5428) in the context of human development. This, again, is focusing on *conditions* for flourishing (or a person's "capabilities" to live their life well), not the definition of flourishing itself (a trick we have seen in [other](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4) [papers](node:c2f0e8a8-3a42-478c-a30c-e479adb75176).) They review the ten capabilities laid out by Martha Nussbaum and note that her argument is not that states need to help citizens flourish in particular ways but that they must *enable* citizens to do so.

With the capabilities approach, the authors can argue that AI surveillance limits four of the ten capabilities laid out by Nussbaum: 
1. The ability to develop and exercise sensory, creative and intellectual capacities
2. The ability to form and live in accordance with an idea of the good life
3. The ability to live and engage with others
4. The ability to take part in collective self-determination

Their argument is that AI surveillance has a chilling effect on individual expression, collective discussion and congregation that amounts to interference and restriction of people's abilities to *develop and exercise* the above capabilities. They don't provide any solutions or options for putting this approach into practice, but they do emphasize that "facilitating identity development" is critical to democratic society and that measuring this development (as well as tangible harms to it) is nontrivial.
attributes.abstract: Abstract AI-enabled State surveillance capabilities are likely to exert chilling effects whereby individuals modify their behavior due to a fear of the potential consequences if that behavior is observed. The risk is that chilling effects drive individuals towards the mainstream, slowly reducing the space for personal and political development. This could prove devastating for individuals’ ability to freely develop their identity and, ultimately, for the evolution and vibrancy of democratic society. As it stands, human rights law cannot effectively conceptualize this cumulative, longer-term, harm, and so cannot accurately evaluate the cost/benefit of AI tools, risking irreparable harm. As chilling effects impact individuals’ ability to live a good, self-determined life, the concept of human flourishing is relevant. This article engages with Aristotelian naturalism, the life-satisfaction approach, and the capabilities approach to determine which best resonates with the concept of identity as relevant to chilling effects and human rights law. It concludes that the capabilities approach may overcome some of the problems associated with the human rights law approach and may provide a framework capable of capturing both the intricate processes of free identity development and of conceptualizing the harm linked to AI surveillance. The challenge, however, is to ‘operationalize’ this approach.

nodes.label: Does a Person Have a Right to Attention? Depends on What She is Doing

attributes.title: Does a Person Have a Right to Attention? Depends on What She is Doing
attributes.summary: The area of human rights is fascinating and seemingly infinitely parseable! This paper focuses on *attention rights*, which, as the authors note, can be debated at length – some scholars argue that the right to attention exists, while others argue that it's attentional *privacy* that the attention economy jeopardizes. The authors try to avoid this debate by focusing on the real-world examples of students taking exams and drivers driving on the road. They argue that in fact, what we care about are *concentration rights* – the student and driver's rights to concentrate on a task for a duration of time without having their attention impacted – and *attentiveness duties* – the driver's duty to, for example, not watch videos as they drive. I have a few qualms with this paper, as these definitions feel somewhat unenforceable (i.e., enforcing a right to concentration or duty to attentiveness seems to conflict with other rights in many cases) and the authors themselves admit they are situation-dependent.
attributes.abstract: Abstract It has been debated whether the so-called attention economy , in which the attention of agents is measured and sold, jeopardizes something of value. One strand of this discussion has focused on so-called attention rights, asking: should attention be legally protected, either by introducing novel rights or by extending the scope of pre-existing rights? In this paper, however, in order to further this discussion, we ask: How is attention already protected legally? In what situations does a person have the right to attention under current law? Unlike (Chomanski, Neuroethics 16:1–11, 2023), who discusses an overall right to attention, or (Puri, Rutgers Law Record 48:206–221, 2021), who discusses an overall right to attentional privacy, in this paper we focus on two types of situations in which a person’s attention is already protected by legal regulation. Sustained attention-requiring tasks can be jeopardized by distractions whereas attentiveness to certain kind of stimuli can be jeopardized by immersive stimuli. That is why distractions are regulated in situations where an agent has what we call a concentration right and immersive stimuli are regulated in situations where an agent has what we call a duty to be attentive. The further analysis of these situations provides an understanding of the legal means by which attention is already regulated, which can be helpful when thinking about how it should be regulated in the future.

nodes.label: Non-voluntary BCI explantation: assessing possible neurorights violations in light of contrasting mental ontologies

attributes.title: Non-voluntary BCI explantation: assessing possible neurorights violations in light of contrasting mental ontologies
attributes.summary: I didn't go beyond the abstract for this paper because it focuses on a case of an implanted brain-computer interface, which is beyond the scope of this Field Guide. But I've seen [Ienca](node:a9dc5f33-eec8-424d-b536-784358f03a8b) cited often in more relevant papers on neurorights so am adding this to the Guide as a pointer for anyone who's interested in diving deeper.
attributes.abstract: In research involving patients with implantable brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), there is a regulatory gap concerning post-trial responsibilities and duties of sponsors and investigators towards implanted patients. In this article, we analyse the case of patient R, who underwent non-voluntary explantation of an implanted BCI, causing a discontinuation in her sense of agency and self. To clarify the post-trial duties and responsibilities involved in this case, we first define the ontological status of the BCI using both externalist (EXT) and internalist (INT) theories of cognition. We then give particular focus to the theories of extended and embedded cognition, hence considering the BCI either as a constitutive component of the patient's mind or as a causal supporter of her brain-based cognitive capacities. We argue that patient R can legitimately be considered both as an embedded and extended cognitive agent. Then, we analyse whether the non-voluntary explantation violated patient R's (neuro)rights to cognitive liberty, mental integrity, psychological continuity and mental privacy. We analyse whether and how different mental ontologies may imply morally relevant differences in interpreting these prima facie neurorights violations and the correlational duties of sponsors and investigators. We conclude that both mental ontologies support the identification of emerging neurorights of the patient and give rise to post-trial obligations of sponsors and investigators to provide for continuous technical maintenance of implanted BCIs that play a significant role in patients' agency and sense of self. However, we suggest that externalist mental ontologies better capture patient R's self-conception and support the identification of a more granular form of mental harm and associated neurorights violation, thus eliciting stricter post-trial obligations.

nodes.label: Neurorights, Mental Privacy, and Mind Reading

attributes.title: Neurorights, Mental Privacy, and Mind Reading
attributes.summary: This paper is focused on neurorights in the context of neurotechnologies, but the author argues that "mind reading" is not restricted to neurotechnology and can in fact be done by picking up on clues to what someone is thinking or aggregating digital data that point to states of mind. It may be relevant as we get farther into the discussion on LLM assistants and shared mental modeling.
attributes.abstract: Abstract A pressing worry in the ongoing neurorights debate is the language used to advocate for newly proposed rights. This paper addresses this concern by first examining the partial and ambiguous associations between mind reading and neurotechnology, often cited by advocates in support of the right to mental privacy. Secondly, it addresses the conceptual foundations of mind reading, distinguishing between natural, digital, and neurotechnological forms. These distinctions serve to highlight the normative parallels in privacy vulnerabilities between neurotechnology and other mind-reading methods, with an emphasis on multimodal digital systems. I suggest that authentic safeguards for the mental realm demand an expansion of the protective ambit beyond brain-targeted devices to recognize the spectrum of mind-reading applications. Ultimately, this urges re-evaluation of the scope and justification of a right to mental privacy owing to the need for coherent frameworks in an increasingly interconnected digital landscape.

nodes.label: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development

attributes.title: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development

nodes.label: AI deskilling is a structural problem

attributes.title: AI deskilling is a structural problem
attributes.summary:
In this paper, Ferdman lays out the following concerns around AI and deskilling:

1. AI can lead to deskilling, not only in profession-specific skills but in life skills like organizing and planning.
2. Deskilling diminishes our abilities in the "arts of personhood," including our epistemic, moral, social and creative capacities.
3. Deskilling is structural, not an individual responsibility.

Ferdman argues that, for example, if workplaces prioritize short-term profits over long-term cognitive ability, then individuals don't have much of a choice about whether to preserve their cognitive skills in cases where individual instances of offloading are more profitable. Her term for these environments is "capacity-hostile": the idea that environments don't just fail to encourage our capacities but actively discourage their cultivation and practice.
attributes.abstract: Abstract Many artificial intelligence tools replace or stand to replace human activity, via automated decision-making, recommender systems and content generation. The more artificial intelligence (AI) replaces valuable human activity, the more it risks deskilling humans of their human capacities. This paper argues for applying a structural perspective to this phenomenon. It introduces the concept of ‘capacity-hostile environments’ to identify instances where AI mediation impedes human capacity cultivation. The analysis moves beyond individual responsibility that agents have to cultivate their human capacities, demonstrating how AI’s influence creates systemic conditions that could inhibit the development and exercise of human capacities by undermining the process of capacity cultivation. Drawing on the philosophy of skill as well as social epistemology, this paper argues that capacity cultivation (skilling) includes acquiring agential control over the capacities, inculcated through a long, gradual process of habituation. Habituation, in turn, depends on learning from others: the ‘know how’ of the skill, as well as a shared understanding of the value of the skill. AI mediation risks undermining the quality of the conditions for capacity habituation, leading to capacity impoverishment. By exploring the role of AI in mediating human activity, the paper highlights the need to evaluate AI applications based on their conduciveness or hostility to capacity cultivation. Ultimately, it calls for a critical reflection on the values inherent in AI socio-technical systems and emphasizes the societal obligation to foster capacity-conducive environments in the age of AI.

attributes.description: Gradual disempowerment is the idea that even incremental improvements in AI capabilities can undermine human influence over large-scale systems that society depends on, including the economy, culture, and nation-states. (Definition from Kulveit et al.)

All sorts of discussions on human rights in the context of AI and other digital technologies. Much of this literature is around neurotechnologies, which are not in scope for this Guide, but the arguments are quite relevant to LLMs.

A term that usually deals specifically with mental privacy, mental integrity and cognitive liberty as it relates to neurotechnologies, i.e., technologies that can be used to read and influence brain activity. Some discussions of neurorights also involve other forms of influence (e.g., attention capture by social media platforms), especially in the context of "freedom of thought" or "self-determination."

The neurorights community proposes mental integrity as "a right over certain parts or functions of the body, that is, the brain" and note that it is similar but distinct from bodily integrity because, e.g., non-invasive brain stimulation can cause mental interference with little to no changes to brain anatomy. [Zuk](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4) extends the definition to include the capacities for affect, cognition and agency, and notes it as being fundamental for autonomy.
