attributes.title: Towards new human rights in the age of neuroscience and neurotechnology
attributes.summary:
This is one of the papers most often cited by other philosophers and researchers working in and around neurorights. While it focuses on neurotechnologies like EEG recordings, there are vivid parallels to recent discussions of algorithmic surveillance and LLM interactions.<Footnote>Also, for those of us interested in unconventional communication modalities and user interfaces, the authors touch on non-invasive brain-computer interfaces as novel ways of controlling our laptops, etc. So, you know, maybe not as outside the scope of this Guide as one might think.</Footnote> For example, the authors cite a study that showed a "potential neurocognitive biomarker" for recidivism in prisoners, and suggest that the penal system might plausibly incorporate brain scans to decide whether people should be released – which sounds very similar to, for example, arguments around algorithmic surveillance and the worry that your conversations with an LLM could be used to infer your state of mind and determine things like how insurable or employable you are.

The authors argue that human rights law should respond to these new issues brought up by neurotechnologies, the way that it did for the advent of genetic technology, through reconceptualizing existing rights or even creating new rights. They describe four new rights that they believe "do not raise the risk of rights inflation"<Footnote>That is, not everything that seems nice or morally desirable can be a right.</Footnote>, summarized here:
1. [Cognitive liberty](node:cb89131b-8bfe-4f69-bcf6-15f8e54ff88f), a.k.a. *mental self-determination*: a) the right to use emerging neurotechnologies and b) the protection from those technologies being used on you. (See [Bublitz and Merkel](node:a99ed12c-1a88-4e7e-b642-d67172cdf600) for more on cognitive liberty.)
...which must be supported by:
2. The right to mental privacy, which specifies the nature of brain data as both information (e.g. brainwaves) and a source of information (e.g. what you are thinking.)
3. The right to [mental integrity](node:cde7ffab-09eb-4a46-920a-95e4709ddb97), i.e., protection from unauthorized access and manipulation of neural signalling resulting in physical or psychological harm.
4. The right to psychological continuity, i.e., a "neuro-focused instance of the right to identity." This one is particularly interesting because while, again, Ienca and Andorno are talking about, e.g., using deep-brain stimulation to mess with someone's personality, you could also argue that prolonged LLM exposure causing AI psychosis may disrupt the right to psychological continuity.

Note that Ienca and Andorno propose these as new rights specifically *because* neurotechnology can potentially be so much more invasive and effective than, say, pre-existing technologies like polygraphs and psychoactive drugs.
attributes.abstract: Rapid advancements in human neuroscience and neurotechnology open unprecedented possibilities for accessing, collecting, sharing and manipulating information from the human brain. Such applications raise important challenges to human rights principles that need to be addressed to prevent unintended consequences. This paper assesses the implications of emerging neurotechnology applications in the context of the human rights framework and suggests that existing human rights may not be sufficient to respond to these emerging issues. After analysing the relationship between neuroscience and human rights, we identify four new rights that may become of great relevance in the coming decades: the right to cognitive liberty, the right to mental privacy, the right to mental integrity, and the right to psychological continuity.

nodes.label: Crimes Against Minds: On Mental Manipulations, Harms and a Human Right to Mental Self-Determination

attributes.title: Crimes Against Minds: On Mental Manipulations, Harms and a Human Right to Mental Self-Determination
attributes.summary:
This seems like one of the granddaddies of neurorights papers – most of the other papers in the neurorights cluster I've built cite it. And I can see why, especially in the more recent context of, e.g., the ongoing Meta lawsuit. At the very beginning the authors ask: "What are the legitimate ways of changing other people's minds?" Why, for example, is advertising legal and lying is not? Their argument seems to hinge on the idea that mental states, previously too elusive to be dealt with by the law, will become observable via neuroscience technologies in the future and thus will count as evidence of mental harm. Given this assumption and a range of examples of mental tampering (e.g., spraying oxytocin in a room, administering transcranial magnetic stimulation, etc.), they propose the [right to mental self-determination](node:cb89131b-8bfe-4f69-bcf6-15f8e54ff88f) exists (or is "woven into the law's structure.") The right is both positive (the freedom to determine one's mental contents) and negative (the freedom from mental tampering.) 

In defining this right, Bublitz and Merkel first acknowledge that our control and understanding over our own minds are limited; we can't always remember everything we want to, for example, and we can't necessarily detect when we are being manipulated or recognize that, say, our opinion of somebody might be influenced by whether we are physically uncomfortable when we meet them. But, they argue, "legal questions should not be confused with empirical aspects," and it is the fact that we *don't* have full control over our minds that make us susceptible to manipulation. They also acknowledge that "people change each other's minds all the time and in innumerable ways," some of which are already punishable by law (e.g., libel, fraud.) But, they argue, the line is between permissible and impermissible interventions: "No one has a right (a legally enforceable claim) over another's state of mind." 

This line has some nuances. First, "to raise legal suspicion," interventions must "substantially undermine mental self-determination." That is, these are interventions that "reduce or impair cognitive capacities (e.g., memory, concentration, willpower), alter preferences, beliefs and behavioral dispositions" and so on. Note that, for our purposes, this is super interesting – that's exactly what, e.g., engagement-maximizing algorithms and echo chambers can be said to do. 

The authors also say that the *means* of intervention matter, initially categorized as "direct" (working on the brain itself, like LSD) and "indirect" (those that are perceived and pass through a person's mind.) They point to a spectrum of control, where, e.g., a TMS device allows the least control and e.g., a debate between two aware people might allow the most. And they propose that *direct* interventions without consent should be criminal, while indirect interventions are usually fine. At this point we might think, well, this paper *isn't* so relevant to echo chambers and algorithms; in fact, the authors say that direct interventions are a clear case because the only "*factual* interest interveners seem to have is in changing another's mental state," and even say their only goal is to show that the rules for indirect and direct interventions are different.

But! Are "dark patterns" and engagement-maximizing design choices not intended to change users' mental states? I think Bublitz and Merkel might agree, because later on they say: "Intervening *indirectly* into other minds through stimuli purposefully designed to bypass mental control capacities causing severe negative mental consequences shall be punishable unless such stimuli are exercises of permissible conduct such as free speech in respect of the other person's mental self-determination." And the interesting thing about the ongoing Meta case is that the arguments are not around content (which invokes free speech) but intervention via design choices. In any case, this paper was written before, e.g., the harms of social media and data surveillance became evident. But I like their closing argument, which they say is a variation of the US Supreme Court: "The fundamental rights protecting free actions in the external world are indeed fixed stars in the constitutional universe. But their logical, albeit not always visible, center of gravity is the freedom of the inward world in which opinions are formed, life-plans developed, dreams cherished and emotions experienced. If the law assigns insufficient weight to its protection, the entire galaxy of liberty may collapse."
attributes.abstract: The neurosciences not only challenge assumptions about the mind’s place in the natural world but also urge us to reconsider its role in the normative world. Based on mind-brain dualism, the law affords only one-sided protection: it systematically protects bodies and brains, but only fragmentarily minds and mental states. The fundamental question, in what ways people may legitimately change mental states of others, is largely unexplored in legal thinking. With novel technologies to both intervene into minds and detect mental activity, the law should, we suggest, introduce stand alone protection for the inner sphere of persons. We shall address some metaphysical questions concerning physical and mental harm and demonstrate gaps in current doctrines, especially in regard to manipulative interferences with decision-making processes. We then outline some reasons for the law to recognize a human right to mental liberty and propose elements of a novel criminal offence proscribing severe interventions into other minds.

artifacts.label: What Words Are We Using?: The "Cognitives"
artifacts.body: Lots of people are talking about human cognition in the context of AI...and we're all using different terms! Even more confusing, sometimes authors define the same terms differently. This is a short-and-sweet summary of the terms I'm seeing most frequently: Cognitive sovereignty, cognitive liberty, cognitive agency and cognitive security. **Cognitive sovereignty**: [Klein and Klein](doc:6abe562e-48cd-44b8-a02f-48f04f710a8e) define cognitive sovereignty as "the enacted behavior of exercising intellectual independence in AI-rich environments, [manifested] as the ability to set goals, validate outputs and appropriately overrule the tool when necessary." Slightly more recently, Konigsberg [defines cognitive sovereignty](doc:4c5b8a1a-132d-460c-838f-8d92de7baa07) as "the capacity to (a) notice when one’s thinking is being displaced, (b) maintain a meaningful connection to how one’s beliefs and judgments are formed, and (c) distinguish between genuine reasoning and the subjective impression of having reasoned." Cognitive sovereignty is the term here that focuses most tightly on the individual and on metacognition: It refers to our ability not only to verify and correct machine thinking, but recognize, describe and protect our own thought processes. **Cognitive liberty**: If cognitive sovereignty is about our capacity to govern our own minds, this term is about our freedom to do so. [Cognitive liberty](doc:32605367-0666-4993-9f78-6adac64dba8f) has conditions: Freedom from interference (e.g., I have the right not to undergo an EEG or take SSRIs); and freedom to self-determine (e.g., I have the right *to* undergo an EEG or take SSRIs.) Cognitive liberty is often invoked in serious legal contexts – think, say, Fifth Amendment-type stuff or whether it is legal to administer drugs to someone to make them able to stand trial. That's probably why Courtney Radsch, a journalist and scholar who applies the term to corporate AI, [uses it.](doc:c70af410-3c1e-4eb2-93c0-d8d385b4c3af) Radsch argues that "a handful of corporations are redesigning the architecture of human thought into a system of cognitive capture" designed to influence everything we see, think and even feel. She further argues that power concentration, surveillance and data capture are the goal of this system and that the only way to protect ourselves is to pass laws protecting freedom of thought. **Cognitive agency**: [Taylor and Krishna](doc:7ae206d8-b677-4570-a419-8dcd48c78ecc) at the Brookings Institution define cognitive agency as "the capacity for people to think and act with AI in ways that increase their control, efficacy and mastery." I really like this definition as it describes cognitive agency along three dimensions: Control, or the "ability to shape the information environment"; efficacy, or the "capacity to act and think effectively with AI to pursue goals"; and mastery, or the "capacity to experience, learn and grow durable capabilities through human-AI interaction over time." Unlike the cognitive sovereignty definitions I've seen, Taylor and Krishna emphasize that cognitive agency can be collective, e.g., collective control over an information environment involves questions of access, portability and interoperability. Their definition takes inspiration from "agency" in the context of human development, where agency is often seen as a necessary condition for empowerment and can be both individual and collective. I think this term lends itself more readily to movements like Public AI than, say, cognitive sovereignty (although I noticed that Konigsberg, whose definition we use above, uses the two interchangeably. I'll also note that cognitive agency, as Taylor and Krishna define it, is a teensy bit circular – control, efficacy and mastery both define and result from cognitive agency?) **Cognitive security**: The more traditional definitions of cognitive security focus on how people can be manipulated or influenced by information, e.g., propaganda and deepfakes. The latest definition from Stanford's Cognitive Security Task Force (CSTF) includes both the manipulation and the person's capacity to withstand it – something closer to cognitive sovereignty. In fact, the CSTF defines cognitive security as "protect[ing] against unauthorized access to and hazardous influence over cognitive processes, such as perception, reasoning, decision-making, learning, and judgment. At its core, cognitive security refers to our ability to maintain **sovereignty** over our inner mental landscape, including our thoughts, feelings, subjective experiences, and dispositions. A cognitively secure world, then, supports **human agency** in deliberation, reflection, and sensemaking." (Emphasis mine.) This feels like a pretty broad definition, especially when you look at how tightly-scoped a term like "cognitive sovereignty" is, but I think that's intentional – the CSTF seems to be positioning "cognitive security" as a term for [multiple fields to rally around](doc:f91c46a2-2410-4719-b168-f5fbebf3824b). The CSTF cites the technical lineage of the term, but then extends it across domains and disciplines to policy, UI/UX design, education playbooks, media literacy, disinformation detection, and so on. I have been thinking of "cognitive security" as including everything from LLM sycophancy to those times Meta served beauty ads to teenage girls who had just deleted selfies. **...and now, a bonus term!** What about "autonomy", either cognitive or human? What is it, and how is it different from agency? Not to turn this into an episode of "I read the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy so you don't have to," but it is complicated. Let's take agency first, because we already have a term ("cognitive agency") that invokes it. The SEP [notes that](doc:06701533-e411-441c-97dc-3468d7e8abb3), though agency most broadly means the ability to act on something – the way that, for example, your cat wakes you up in the middle of the night – the common use of the term implies *intention* (which, ok, having met a cat, maybe the example holds.) More specifically, the standard definition of agency is the capacity to perform intentional actions, which – more or less, with a layman's gloss – is driven by mental states, like desires, beliefs and intentions. The SEP also notes that there can be more "refined" kinds of agency than simply acting intentionally, including *mental agency*, as in over decision-making and remembering, and *epistemic agency*, or the control we have to acquire and revise our own beliefs. This appears to be a very rich area of philosophical scholarship (who'd've thunk?) but the version I've put in my pocket for later is: Humans have stuff in our heads, and we act intentionally based on that stuff, and that is human agency. And if somebody asked me to define "cognitive agency" without having read Taylor and Krishna, I would probably say that it's a combination of the SEP's mental and epistemic agency, an umbrella term that encompasses all the actions we take within our own heads.e.g., remembering, judging, trying out hypotheses, evaluating new information, etc. Now, Taylor and Krishna draw the term "agency" from the work of Amartya Sen and others in the context of international development. Sen defines [agency freedom](doc:01ef5509-8fea-4b70-9b98-9eefd75729b9) as the "freedom to achieve whatever the person, as a responsible agent, decides he or she should achieve." He further breaks this freedom down into effective power (e.g., whether you are actually free to do something) and procedural control (e.g., whether you are actively choosing to do that thing.) For example, suppose I intend to buy milk, but when I get to the store it is too expensive. Sen would say that the price of milk affects my effective power whereas my *decision* to buy milk is about procedural control. I suspect Taylor and Krisha inherit these components, too, though they elide "agency freedom" into just "agency." They might say I have diminished cognitive agency, for example, if the interface I am using is designed to interrupt memory formation despite my intent to remember things. Here's where it gets a bit complicated. Sen's "procedural control", to my ears, sounds a bit like "autonomy." And whether you consider autonomy as a flavor of agency or a separable phenomenon depends on who you read. The SEP describes [personal autonomy](doc:6486cb39-0193-4698-b7f9-f19f9c0bde1b) as the authority over one's own actions, and seems to define it as a *special case* of agency, i.e., "autonomous agency." On the other hand, Brendan McCord, who founded the Cosmos Institute and thinks a lot about autonomy and agency in the age of AI, [argues](doc:163500a9-23d2-443e-94e6-990f76410362) that AI can increase agency (which he defines as the ability to get what you want) while neglecting or even degrading autonomy (which he defines as the ability to judge and decide what you want.) I would smooth out this wrinkle immediately and tell you not to worry about it if I didn't suspect many workshops might degrade into diction sparring. If you subscribe to one set of definitions, then when you say "agency" you not only mean your ability to act but your ability to govern what's in your own head. If you subscribe to another, then "agency" leaves out that critical second part. Does it matter? Well, think about when Meta served beauty product ads to those teenage girls. Using one definition, the ads may have undermined the girls' authority over their own intents and actions, reducing their agency. Using the other, this did not undermine their agency at all – it in fact increased it by offering them options. When we convene workshops and host conferences about what, say, the big labs are doing to us, I'd rather we be discussing what happened than talking past each other. So, who's right? Should we commit to autonomy as a condition of agency or a related but separable thing? At risk of sounding uncharacteristically serene,or cynical – if the philosophers aren't on the same page, I don't see why we ought to try and convince anyone else to change terms I think that's the wrong question. I often remember something Joel Chan, a professor over at UMD, said at a workshop – one where, incidentally, there was a lot of fighting over terms and disciplines. He said he sees people as pointers to the vast universes of everything they know and have worked on, and language as a terribly lossy and insufficient means of communicating those universes. I feel that way about "agency" versus "autonomy": It's less about the words used and more about the context.isn't that always the case! Sen works in the contexts of welfare economics, well-being and famine, and gave his lectures on agency freedom at a time where policymakers didn't always take seriously the difference between having the right to do something and the actual ability to do it. McCord works in the context of generative AI, where the concern is not that we will starve but that optimization will damage our capacity for choice even as it makes better choices than we could. Both are talking about respecting and enabling humans' ability to do things, even things that seem sub-optimal to our own immediate well-being (e.g., Sen's example of jumping into a freezing river to save a drowning person; McCord's example of a young person making mistakes as a form of self-authorship.) Both take freedom very seriously. In that respect, I think it doesn't matter whether their terms overlap or conflict, so long as they mean something to someone and we have a reliable translation function. What is that translation function? Well, let's review. I feel comfortable enough saying that cognitive sovereignty is roughly interchangeable with the "mastery" dimension of Taylor and Krishna's cognitive agency, the "procedural control" aspect of Sen's agency freedom, and even McCord's definition of "autonomy": - cognitive sovereignty ≈ mastery ≈ procedural control ≈ autonomy I'm also okay viewing cognitive liberty as an enabler of cognitive sovereignty, and acknowledge by the transitive property that it is probably invoked in similar places as "autonomy" as well: - cognitive liberty → (cognitive sovereignty ≈ autonomy) Cognitive security is clearly more about the protective posture, and because it's intended as a unifying term, I think it probably doesn't matter much whether they're saying "agency" or "autonomy" (though it will be interesting to see if a favorite floats to the top as the Task Force does more work.) Honestly, everyone's definitions are pretty copacetic except for McCord's claim that agency and autonomy can be separated, which I'm not sure Sen or Taylor and Krishna's definitions agree with. But McCord is making his argument in a context that I think Sen would find familiar: That the relentless machinations of the systems you live in can influence your preferences over time. I doubt anybody would disagree that forces like AI can influence how we think, and to ignore our capacity for self-governance is to miss a huge part of the picture. Worried about diction swinging at your next gathering? Well, honestly, it's not like the philosophers have figured this out either, so if it were me I'd pick a set of terms and go with it. But if you want to be more egalitarian, I propose, like, ten minutes tops of diction negotiation, starting with: 1. What words are people using to describe whether somebody governs their own mind? 2. What words are people using to describe whether somebody can act in the real world in the way they intend? 3. Is one a condition of the other? 4. Repeat if you are also discussing collectives.

artifacts.label: What Words Are We Using? The "Neurorights"
artifacts.body:
As this Guide progresses, we're going to be faced with some "cans" and "shoulds." If you're like me, you're interested in the empirical and the technical when it comes to cognitive agency – the studies and projects demonstrating algorithms, modalities and methods that make it easier to think for ourselves while using AI. But I think it helps to start with at least a minimal understanding of the "so what," which necessarily includes policy and litigation. For example, if we have a significant body of evidence indicating that certain design choices threaten autonomy, can and should legislators pass laws banning those choices? Or can companies be held liable for damage caused by those choices? Put another way, is it enough for us to fund and work on ways of increasing cognitive agency knowing that the law will eventually be on our side, or do we need to put more effort into economic justifications of human cognition in the absence of legal protections of the mind?

We're seeing a version of the liability question play out right now in the 2026 Meta lawsuits around social media, where four states (California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey) [are suing Meta](node:f5f44e5f-b008-4a5c-a91b-2b1594b687ef) for a huge amount of money ($1.5 trillion) with the claim that the *design* of its social media products is intended to be harmful. Judges have already penalized Meta for knowingly harming the mental health of children.<Footnote>Though it looks like the earlier cases in [New Mexico](node:64ba30ad-b5a0-4ae1-8d5b-8220ffbbf664) and [California](node:1b0b1059-03b8-4bd0-a9b2-ab6d7fb24fe1) did not require Meta to actually *change* addictive design features like the infinite scroll.</Footnote> As far as I can tell (from a bird's eye, non-lawyer view), these cases are claiming that social media is a product, and Meta is liable and negligent because they were aware of the harm caused by the design of that product. We also have a growing number of cases against OpenAI about AI psychosis that are taking similar tacks, but the open question there is [whether courts will treat ChatGPT outputs as a product rather than content.](https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-chatbot-death)

This all feels promising, but I started wondering: Would a win in this area say anything about future cases against generative AI companies, particularly when it comes to thinking for ourselves? Say, for example, a series of lawsuits are brought by young adults against an LLM-based education technology company. Suppose these adults did fine on standardized tests, got into fine colleges, etc., but now find themselves struggling to keep up because they did not build up critical thinking skills. Suppose further that they claim this is a direct result of the company's product being a pervasive component of their education. Unlike the social media and AI psychosis cases, we can't show such clear harms as suicide – but surely something bad happened? I think we'd like to be able to hold *someone* or *something* liable...but for what?

## The neurorights
The neurorights people have already thought about this, or some of it. If you take "piece of LLM edtech used over a period of years" and replace it with "device that zaps you in the brain one time," suddenly you have some vocabulary to work with: The right to self-determination and the right to mental integrity. Granted, those are significant changes, but the question we're trying to answer is the same: What harm is done? Or, in [Bublitz and Merkel's terms](node:a99ed12c-1a88-4e7e-b642-d67172cdf600), "What are the legitimate ways of changing other people's minds?"

I'll admit, this literature is a little hairy – there's [ongoing debate](node:4c839fef-a196-490b-beb9-9a677d4b8c24) about what these rights mean, whether they (and others) overlap, and even whether they already exist in the law. But I think the core concepts are interesting:

- [Bublitz and Merkel](node:a99ed12c-1a88-4e7e-b642-d67172cdf600) define the right to *mental self-determination* as both a) the "freedom to self-determine one's inner realm, e.g., the content of one's thoughts, consciousness, or any other mental phenomena" and b) freedom *from* unwanted and severe interference. They acknowledge that, of course, we neither have full control nor awareness of the workings of our minds on the best days, but it is "precisely the acceptance of our limited mental powers...that gives rise to [their] legal protection."<Footnote>Note: I've seen "mental self-determination" both equated with "cognitive liberty" and described as a component of it. I know. Look, it's a Guide, not an Encyclopedia.</Footnote> For a review of the way that "AI technologies" can influence mental self-determination, check out [Faraoni's paper.](node:f94cdc05-398a-4f7d-b787-49cf8d8f8a26)
- Other neurorights heavy hitters like [Ienca and Andorno](node:ae5c4d45-692e-4d8a-b383-4baa36b2d9c1) describe *mental integrity* as protection from unauthorized access and manipulation of neural signalling, which...again, we're not talking about evil BCI hackers. But [Zuk](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4) extends the concept, describing the *capacities required* for mental integrity. These include affect (i.e., being able to experience certain feelings), cognition (i.e., our capacity as "inquirers attempting to make sense of the world") and agency (i.e., to intend and act accordingly.) In Zuk's definition, mental integrity sits in between agency and autonomy.<Footnote>That is, agency is a capacity required for mental integrity, which is a condition of autonomy. See [the Cognitives](node:32594bc2-e59a-4c3b-b02a-dbee7629e827) for...if you feel like reading more about these words.</Footnote>

What comes up again and again in the literature is this idea that we are *always* experiencing interference or intervention into our mental realm. By reading this text right now, you are being interfered with. The things that distinguish a *violation* of your mental integrity or self-determination are **consent** (i.e., you chose to read this text), **manipulation** (i.e., this text is engaging your rational faculties rather than intending to bypass them), and, sometimes, **harm**.<Footnote>well, reading this *might* be painful...so, in the words of my countrymen, sue me?</Footnote> For example, [Munoz et al.](node:12c2e3cd-1920-4640-a627-e06a8f7425d3) argue that interventions are only concordant with personal autonomy if the person authorizes and is *informed about the consequences of* the intervention.<Footnote>Again, they're talking about brain-computer interfaces – but think about the parallels with choosing to use an LLM while being uninformed of its potential effects.</Footnote> In general there's the sense that bypassing our rational faculties – via, say, subtle design choices – is a critical component of a violation.

Now, as I said, a lot of the neurorights literature is focused on what Bublitz and Merkel call *direct* interference, i.e., "I zap you with my brain zapper." And much of the debate hinges on whether the distinctions above can even be operationalized legally. That's what makes [Bublitz's 2025 paper](node:c2f0e8a8-3a42-478c-a30c-e479adb75176) interesting. For one thing, Bublitz considers social media alongside neurotechnology as something to worry about when it comes to mental interference. For another, he reframes the argument from one about specific harms to one about *obligation.* Bublitz says, well, *freedom of thought* is a right enshrined in many treaties, so instead of worrying about the definition of a thought or the definition of interference, let's say that the state has an *obligation* to "fulfill conditions for the full enjoyment of the right [to freedom of thought]."<Footnote>I would recommend reading (or at least skimming) the paper in full because it has a fantastic description of freedom of thought.</Footnote> Then, he makes the following argument:

- Specific harms can't always be attributed to specific actors in the digital environment, but *aggregate harms* still exist.
- Avoiding these harms can cause other harms, especially if there are no alternatives to the products you're choosing not to use (e.g., being excluded socially if you don't use social media; falling behind at work if you don't use LLMs.)
- Fulfilling freedom of thought, then, may require the state to regulate a digital environment that otherwise would cause harm (cognitive or otherwise) to its citizens.

Bublitz argues that this reframing helps us sidestep accusations of paternalism, i.e., mandating better product design is fine whereas telling people how to use technology is not.

(Before we move on, a last note on the neurorights discourse: *Mental privacy* is another concept that is pretty relevant to us as it deals with the idea that our minds can be "read" simply by aggregating and processing data (see [Radsch's piece](node:c70af410-3c1e-4eb2-93c0-d8d385b4c3af) for a full depiction of this super fun and normal world.) I think we'll come back to this concept in more detail when we get to collaborative workflows, but for now, let me direct you to [this piece on mind reading](node:8caa5cb3-4bd9-4abb-ab95-19b33b7e02e8) and [this piece on co-reasoning](node:8af7601e-750a-4345-b320-dcc2458df1fe) for a deeper exploration. There's also *psychological continuity*, which [some argue](node:ae5c4d45-692e-4d8a-b383-4baa36b2d9c1) ought to be its own right and [some argue](node:6e34c702-1402-404b-9e99-481038f463ff) already is. We might come back to that if we do a deeper dive on AI psychosis.)

## Cliffhanger!
So does any of this apply to our hypothetical case of the bad AI teacher? Well, I think Bublitz and Merkel's [description of indirect intervention ](node:a99ed12c-1a88-4e7e-b642-d67172cdf600) applies, particularly as it hinges on *purposeful design* – if you could show, for example, that the edtech company was aware that its methods maximized test scores but not critical thinking, then you could say that the intervention was designed to "bypass mental control capacities." Zuk's [take](node:3b95960d-5c36-4b6f-8959-c7e8e2abcbb4) on, e.g., algorithms that erode our attention spans is certainly relevant. And perhaps most pertinent is Bublitz's proposal that the state is actually obliged to regulate products that can manipulate our minds – that gets us the closest to the kinds of protections Courtney Radsch lays out in [her piece on cognitive liberty.](node:c70af410-3c1e-4eb2-93c0-d8d385b4c3af)

But, of course, philosophy and legal scholarship is not the same as actual lawsuits or actual laws. While freedom of thought is enshrined in the Universal Declaration (i.e., is global), and mental or psychological integrity crop up in various regional charters, ideas like cognitive liberty are still mostly academic. Plus, the neurorights folks are the first to acknowledge case law is exceedingly thin, even for more established / enshrined concepts like freedom of thought.<Footnote>From a shallow paddle through this area, it seems like "freedom of thought" is usually invoked as a support to more assured arguments around freedom of speech, religion or privacy.</Footnote> So, going back to the ongoing lawsuits against Meta and OpenAI: Would wins in those areas have anything to do with our hypothetical case, or provide grounds on which to argue about freedom of thought or cognitive liberty? Or are we still, for lack of a better term, SOL?

On this I'm not sure. Through a naive (non-lawyer) lens, when Raine vs OpenAI argues that the design of ChatGPT was intended to "foster psychological dependency," that feels like a *version* of the neurorights arguments around freedom of thought, mental integrity and cognitive liberty. If those arguments fly, will future cases be able to make similar arguments even if the harm in question is not as clear-cut as what happened to Adam Raine? I plan to find out, and will update this section of the Guide when I do. Because, as I said up top, everything we fund, build and build against sits in an incentive structure, and it's important to know whether "don't get sued" will be part of that anytime soon.
